To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

nine-spined stick-lebacks (Pungitus pungitius L.) can use public information to make foraging decisions, but that they prefer to rely on this information rather than simpler social cues when available.
nine-spined stick-lebacks prefer to rely upon public information over simple social cues, and that this preference allows them to avoid engaging in erroneous information-al cascades.

(a) foraging sticklebacks can use both public information and social cues to make foraging decisions, (b) when only social cues are available, they prefer the patch previously associated more often with more conspecifics than less, and (c) when public information is also available, they preferentially use the public information to make foraging patch choices.
